#1492. Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been announced.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

The charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

It would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

Each of those cases would have to be held individually, potentially leading to years more of litigation. Conversely, if City win their appeal, they too could take legal action against the Premier League the damage caused to their reputation.

There has not yet been an official confirmation of the independent panel’s verdict from the Premier League. The Premier League declined to comment.

However, several sources have told Telegraph Sport that the panel has found City guilty of all but one of the charges they faced. The one that has not been proved is said to be one of the most serious of the 115.

The damning verdict for City is a major new test of fragile UK relations with the United Arab Emirates, with whom bilateral trade was worth £25bn last year. Redacted freedom of information documents, seen by Telegraph Sport, show Abu Dhabi hosted UK government officials including Lord Stockwood, then investment minister, as recently as February. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the City chairman and trusted adviser to the UAE president, was present at the meeting. Government notes from the meeting recorded that he “noted they are very proud of what they have achieved through their investments in Manchester”.

The Government previously caused acrimony among senior leaders in Abu Dhabi after putting forward legislation to ban foreign states from owning UK newspapers and news magazines. The intervention prompted the collapse of a takeover of The Telegraph in April 2024, which was largely funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the owner of City and vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The previous UK government has admitted its embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Foreign Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) in London discussed the charges levelled at City by the Premier League. However it refused to disclose the correspondence.

City have steadfastly maintained they are innocent, promising “irrefutable” evidence in support of their position, and had assembled some of the most expensive lawyers in the country to argue their case. Despite the verdict, the club are understood to be confident that it will win the argument in the end. Senior figures are said to be calm about the latest development, as significant as it seems.

City rebuilt their team this summer and it is understood that signings were brought in on conventional player contracts, rather than terms including clauses triggered in the event of a heavy punishment. Given the club have consistently denied breaching financial regulations, and their deals for new players to work with head coach Enzo Maresca underlines their position.

On Friday, a City spokesman said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Sources close to Pep Guardiola, the former City manager who stepped down last summer after 10 years of remarkable success at the club, including a treble triumph in 2023 and an unprecedented fourth straight league title in 2024, insist he has not been informed of any verdict.

In the days after City were first charged, Guardiola mounted a fierce defence of the club, claiming: “I am fully convinced we will be [proved] innocent.”

The verdict vindicates the Premier League’s decision to launch an investigation after explosive allegations that City had routinely broken financial rules were first made in Der Spiegel in 2018 based on the Football Leaks documents.

Uefa previously accused City of breaches of its financial regulations and announced in 2020 that it was suspending the club from the Champions League for two years for “overstating” sponsorship revenue between 2012 and 2016.

City denied the Uefa charges and, after an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the two-year ban was overturned. Cas found that a number of the claims brought by Uefa had fallen outside a five-year “time bar” and others were “not established”.

It did, however, still impose a €10m fine after ruling that City failed to cooperate with investigators. City had previously also agreed a settlement with Uefa of €20m in 2014 following an investigation into their finances.

Legal experts agreed that the commission’s verdict is far from the end of the case. Yasin Patel, barrister at Church Court Chambers, said: “City’s lawyers will now analyse this decision and look at the options open to them to appeal, which may include procedural impropriety, wrongful interpretation of law, and legal errors – importantly, they can guarantee an appeal.

“Sanctions could include a major fine, points deduction, relegation or even all three. Factoring in whether titles and trophies should be stripped, whether other clubs have been robbed of further revenue and opportunities due to City’s wrongdoings and losses incurred, we safely say that this is only the first chapter of a long-running legal saga that will not end any time soon.”

Ian Hargreaves, partner with specialist disputes firm Quillon Law, said the verdict was “not the end of the story but the beginning of a new phase”, and added: “There is also the question of whether the panel’s decision can withstand a hard-fought appeal, and on what grounds any challenge might be brought. Much will depend on the detail of the panel’s findings and reasoning, which will inevitably be closely scrutinised by both sides.”

Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who won the Ballon d’Or during his trophy-laden spell at the club, said he believed the club were innocent.

“For the players, it’s different than it is for journalists. I can understand all opinions, but we try to stay positive,” the Spain midfielder said while on international duty.

“When you see all the people who worked hard at City to achieve success, you know what we achieved can’t be taken away. It wasn’t paid for with money, but with effort and teamwork. Everything we achieved was deserved; we marked one of the great eras of English football. I believe in the club’s innocence – we already went through this in 2020.”

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said: “I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”

Zohran Kwame Mamdani, the mayor of New York, posted “114” in relation to the charges while former Manchester United players David de Gea and Rio Ferdinand both asked whether they should be due winner’s medals from past seasons.

The Premier League statement in February 2023 said that “a number of alleged breaches” had been referred to an independent commission. It then detailed each specific rule against each season in which the alleged breach took place. The precise number was not clear from the statement and led to varying reports between 115 and 130. Friday’s news suggested the figure was 115.

All the way to 2009-10, the first full season following the club’s takeover by Sheikh Mansour, who is a member of the Abu Dhabi Royal family and the vice president of the United Arab Emirates. There were charges relating to all 14 seasons until the Premier League completed their investigation during the 2022-23 campaign. In that time, City won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Champions League. They have since won another league title – the first club to do so four times in a row – as well as the Uefa Super Cup, the Fifa Club World Cup and the FA Cup and League Cup double last season.

They can be split into five groups. The biggest relates to the seasons from 2009-10 until 2017-18 and the requirement for clubs to provide accurate financial information and act in the utmost good faith.

The next set of rules concern the full disclosure of manager and player payments. The alleged manager breaches related to the period between 2009-10 and 2012-13, when Roberto Mancini was leading the team. The alleged breaches with respect to player payments relate to all of the seasons between 2010-11 and 2015-16.

As well as providing financial detail, clubs were required to meet Uefa and Premier League rules which were designed to bring a club’s spending broadly in line with their income by placing set limits on losses. City were charged with breaches of Uefa’s licencing and financial fair play rules from 2013-14 until 2017-18, and the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules from 2015-16 until 2017-18.

The final set of charges spanned the five seasons during which City were being investigated by the Premier League and rules that require members to cooperate in the utmost good faith by providing information and documents.

A full picture will only emerge when the commission publishes its findings but we know that the Premier League investigation began in December 2018 following allegations in the German newspaper Der Spiegel based on the Football Leaks documents. These included alleged payments to former manager Mancini for consultancy work at an Abu Dhabi-based club that was separate to his regular contract at City.

We also know that City were alleged to have breached rules over setting out image rights payments to players in their club contract. Der Spiegel reported that the Premier League investigation also focused on payments to under-age players, as well as whether club sponsors were paying for commercial deals themselves or a significant proportion was in fact effectively coming from owner Sheikh Mansour.

City have always denied breaking any rules. In response to the Premier League statement about the alleged breaches, they said that they have “irrefutable evidence” to support their position and “look forward to this matter being put to rest once and for all.”

At the start of the hearing in September 2024, Guardiola also said: “Wait for the independent panel. We believe we have not done anything wrong.”

Of the Football Leaks documents, City said: “We will not be providing any comment on out-of-context materials. The attempt to damage the club’s reputation is organised and clear.”

#1491. Romelu Lukaku announces 'bombshell' international retirement: Former Chelsea star, 33, U-turns on his Belgium future - leaving Belgian press stunned

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 08:03 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:49 EST, 16 November 2026

Romelu Lukaku has announced his retirement from international football in a 'bombshell' decision that has left the Belgian press utterly stunned.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United forward, 33, vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament with the Belgium national team, although he now appears to have changed his mind over his future.

Describing his international career as a 'great ride', Lukaku took to social media on Monday morning to break the unexpected news.

'16 years old,' his Instagram statement began. 'For 16 years, I gave everything for the national team. I experienced every possible emotion. I played with fantastic teammates for whom I will always be grateful.

'I want to thank them all. I also want to thank all the coaches for pushing me and giving me the confidence to help the team. It was a great ride, and I enjoyed every moment.

'To the Belgian fans, thank you for the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments. I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing, it was a joy. I am grateful. Thank you.'

Belgium legend Romelu Lukaku has announced his decision to retire from international football

Lukaku vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament

The Belgian forward has fallen down the pecking order and spent a lot of time on the bench

The Belgian veteran accompanied his post with a gallery of photographs from his storied international career, from his debut against Croatia under Dick Advocaat in 2010 to his final chapter wearing the armband.

Lukaku has captained Belgium on a handful of occasions since 2020, alongside the likes of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans.

The 33-year-old forward, who became one of the hottest properties in world football after breaking on the scene at Chelsea, has been a regular fixture in the international set-up for almost two decades.

Spearheading Belgium's golden generation, which included star-studded talents such as De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, Lukaku chalked up an impressive 135 caps for the international team.

He also retires as Belgium's all-time top scorer on 94 goals, just six shy of a century.

Belgian newspapers were caught out by the shock announcement, which was described as an 'unexpected bombshell' by outlet HLN on Monday.

Lukaku's stock within the international set-up has fallen since he promised the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament in January.

After suffering multiple injury setbacks, he featured at the tournament under Rudi Garcia and continued to play a crucial role, scoring three times as a substitute to guide Belgium to the quarter-finals where they were ultimately stopped by eventual champions Spain.

Since Mark van Bommel's appointment in August, following Garcia's departure at the end of his contract, Lukaku has slipped further down the pecking order, with Charles De Ketelaere preferred to lead the line.

Lukaku, pictured with Kevin De Bruyne, was an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1

Axel Witsel sent a heartfelt message to Lukaku on Instagram: 'Thanks for everything, legend'

During Belgium's resounding 4-1 victory over Italy on Sunday, Lukaku warmed the bench as an unused substitute - and wasn't even in the squad to face Turkey three days before.

While Belgium were winning in the second half against the Italians, Lukaku was seen warming up on the sidelines in the hope of featuring for one last time, but unfortunately was not given the opportunity.

VTM NIEUWS anchor Maarten Breckx claimed De Bruyne looked 'concerned' while speaking to Lukaku on the bench, suggesting the former Man City star was unhappy to see his team-mate overlooked.

'When it became clear that he wouldn't be allowed to come on, De Bruyne was talking to him. You could see the concern in his eyes,' he said.

'You could tell, especially from Romelu's attitude, that he was dissatisfied and displeased. He had probably counted on getting some minutes...'

With only Jan Vertonghen and Axel Witsel registering more international caps than Lukaku over their careers, boasting 157 and 140 appearances respectively, Belgium are expected to give the 33-year-old forward a send-off he deserves in the near future.

Witsel, who also called time on his Belgium career this year, was one of the team-mates to celebrate Lukaku's retirement on Instagram.

'Thanks for everything, legend. Thank you, what a journey we've had together,' he wrote.

#1490. Bayern Munich cools the prospect of a new transfer at €100 million

Could Bayern Munich make a new transfer worth 100 million euros to strengthen its squad before the 2028 Champions League final, which will be played at the Allianz Arena? Asked about this possibility after the historic recruitment of Harry Kane in 2023, Herbert Hainer preferred to calm expectations. The Bavarian president assures that the club does not intend to spend considerable sums with the sole objective of playing this final at home. “ Reaching the Champions League final in our stadium would be the icing on the cake. However, it is certain that we will not invest millions of euros just for that day, or for this season “, he explained. If the manager does not explicitly close the door to a new major operation on the transfer market, he insists on the need to maintain a coherent financial strategy, despite Bayern’s ambition to continue to compete with the best European teams.

Herbert Hainer believes in particular that Bayern Munich must compensate for its financial resources lower than those of certain competitors with a more intelligent recruitment policy. “ There are clubs in Europe who simply have more money at their disposal. This is why we must be smarter and better than others “, he continued. To illustrate this strategy, the Bavarian president cited the arrivals of Harry Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Díaz, three operations that were particularly complex to carry out, but which he considers today to be real successes. “ These three players were major challenges to recruit, but they turned out to be real success stories “, he stressed. Hainer also praised the work of CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen, as well as that of Max Eberl and Christoph Freund, who are responsible for the club’s sports policy. A way of reminding us that Bayern intends to continue its development in the long term, without disrupting its strategy for a single European event.

#1489. The top 10 currently active players with the most goals in Europe’s top five leagues

With Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo plying their trade outside Europe these days, who are the players with the most goals to their names still active in Europe’s top five leagues?

There’s some serious goalscoring talent in the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1. The current top 10 features a mix of world-class stars right now and some who peaked a decade ago but are still plugging away.

Here are the top 10 players currently active in Europe’s top five leagues with the most goals in those leagues.

Villarreal captain Moreno has spent his entire career in Spain, playing in La Liga since 2014 after scoring 46 goals in the third tier and 15 in the second tier.

He had a three-year spell with Espanyol but went back to Villarreal in 2018 and is now just three goals away from a century of La Liga goals in their colours alone.

Just ahead of Domenico Berardi and Paulo Dybala as the top active scorer in Serie A is Inter captain Martinez.

Inter brought him to Europe from Racing Club in his native Argentina in 2018 and neither party has looked back since. Martinez was Serie A’s top scorer in 2023-24 and 2025-26.

Kramaric’s first taste of playing in one of Europe’s top five leagues was when he came to the Premier League with Leicester, where he scored a grand total of two goals.

It’s gone better for him in the Bundesliga with Hoffenheim ever since. He joined the German side in 2016 and has reached double figures of goals in nine seasons.

Another one from the category of: not much to write home about in the Premier League, but actually pretty good elsewhere.

Aspas arrived at Liverpool on the back of his debut season in La Liga, when he scored 12 goals for Celta de Vigo. He never scored in the Premier League, before scoring twice back in La Liga on loan at Sevilla and settling permanently with Celta again, going on to score more than 150 more times in the Spanish top flight.

Yep, not only is he still active in Europe’s top five leagues, he’s playing in the Champions League too at the ripe age of 40.

Giroud’s goals have been spread between spells in Ligue 1, the Premier League and Serie A. After a stint in MLS, he came back to Europe in 2025 with Lille, taking his chance to add to his 33 previous Ligue 1 goals (which he got with Montpellier before his Arsenal move).

Give him a couple of years and he’ll be in the top three, you’d imagine.

Haaland is quite simply a goalscoring machine and has been ever since he first featured in one of Europe’s top five leagues, when he went to Borussia Dortmund in 2020.

After his 62 Bundesliga goals, he’s gone on to become a member of the Premier League’s 100 Club while starring for Manchester City.

Back in March 2018, Dzeko became the first player ever to score 50 goals in three of Europe’s top five leagues.

He’d already done it in the Bundesliga with Wolfsburg and the Premier League with Manchester City, before reaching the milestone in Serie A with Roma as well. He later surpassed 100 in the Italian top flight while with Inter.

Still playing at 40, he’s part of Schalke’s squad now, but after helping them win promotion earlier this year, he hasn’t scored for them this season yet. In fact, his last goal in one of Europe’s top five leagues was actually in May 2023.

Aubameyang has also since joined the exclusive group of half-centurions from three of the top five leagues, doing so in the Bundesliga, Premier League and Ligue 1. He was at Marseille in the 2023-24 season when he ticked off the last of the three.

He’ll have his work cut out to reach the milestone in La Liga as well, where he now plies his trade with Deportivo, but he’s having a fine season at the age of 37.

He’s scored five goals so far in the Spanish top flight this season, having previously scored 11 in it for Barcelona.

No surprises who’s in the top two – and it’s in the same order as for the 2026 Ballon d’Or.

Mbappe is one of the best players in the world right now and he’s been doing it for ages. Sure, he’s not won anything of note at Real Madrid yet, but you can’t argue with his goalscoring rates.

He claimed the Pichichi award as La Liga’s top scorer in both of his first two seasons in Spain. Before that, just the 191 goals in Ligue 1 with Monaco and then PSG, making him the sixth highest scorer in the competition’s history and the best this side of 2000.

But like with the Ballon d’Or, it’s Kane in top spot. He’s had a few more years to get the goals than Mbappe, to be fair, but his consistency has been incredible.

When he first emerged in the Tottenham first team, some feared he was a one season wonder. It’s been an awfully long season if that’s the case.

He eventually left Spurs on 213 Premier League goals, more than anyone else except Alan Shearer. Rather than pursue that record, he chose to pursue trophies with Bayern Munich instead, casually reaching 100 Bundesliga goals within 98 games – 31 fewer than the next quickest player to reach the milestone.

Kane’s recent contract extension means there’ll be plenty more goals to come.

#1484. Klopp breaks ranks to savage Infantino: Liverpool legend becomes first boss to turn on FIFA president - who is WORSE than Sepp Blatter - as pressure mounts after World Cup farce

Published: 08:02 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 10:36 EST, 16 November 2026

Jurgen Klopp has called on FIFA's embattled president Gianni Infantino to resign, becoming the first national team manager to do so.

Infantino's reputation took a nosedive after his sycophantic behaviour towards Donald Trump before and during the World Cup - most memorably by awarding him a 'FIFA Peace Prize'.

And it only got worse when his clandestine plot to sell off stakes in the World Cup, a devious scheme which would have banked him millions, was revealed by The Times.

Now Germany manager Klopp has hit out: 'There is now a unanimous consensus that a change would make sense.

'I thought that, after Sepp Blatter, the situation couldn't get any worse - but here we are.

'Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.

Jurgen Klopp has publicly savaged FIFA president Gianni Infantino, becoming the first national team manager to do so

The Germany manager said Infantino - who tried to sell off stakes in the World Cup to his own benefit - is 'worse' than his predecessor Sepp Blatter

'Without a doubt, there are people who truly care about football and have no financial interests,' the former Liverpool manager said.

Infantino has clung on to his job thus far, surviving a crisis summit in Morocco in August, despite intense and widespread opposition.

A total of 90 nations including all of UEFA's teams rebelled, with threats to boycott FIFA competitions, and Infantino's £3.1billion plan fell apart.

But he still maintained a large swell of support among Africa, Asia, and South America - especially after offering each nation £30million if they supported his plan. His opponents pointed out that he could simply have given money from FIFA's cash reserves of roughly £4.5b.

In the pages of this historic newspaper, football legend Luis Figo wrote that 'Infantino must go' and accused him of 'debasing the office of FIFA President'.

FIFA does not have a history of picking good leaders - Blatter resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption, though he was cleared alongside Michel Platini last year.

Infantino now looks well-placed to be re-elected for a fourth term in next March's presidential elections.

The deadline for candidacies to be submitted is November 18.

Philippe Diallo, the French Football Federation president, has agreed to run against Infantino and has the backing of UEFA's executive committee.

'(Diallo has) extensive experience across all levels of the game, having led the organisation representing French professional football clubs, served on the board of the French professional league and within FIFA’s dispute resolution structures, before becoming President of the FFF and a member of the UEFA Executive Committee in 2023,' UEFA said.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega has already announced his intention to be a rival to Infantino.

Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japanese Football Association, is also reportedly set to mount a challenge.

Ex-Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger was touted as a potential challenger but it is understood he told European football’s governing body UEFA that he would not stand.

#1483. Man Utd manager debuts ranked since Sir Alex Ferguson: Pochettino next

After replacing Michael Carrick in the dugout, Mauricio Pochettino starts his reign as Manchester United head coach with a game against Liverpool at Anfield.

Pochettino is set to become the 12th manager to take charge of a United game since Sir Alex Ferguson retired at the end of the 2012/13 season.

We’ve taken a look at how his predecessors fared in their first competitive game in charge of United, ranking them from worst to best.

Following the appointment of Van Gaal and six wins out of six in pre-season, United fans were full of optimism ahead of the 2014/15 campaign.

But the mood changed just 28 minutes into the season when Ki Sung-yueng gave Swansea City the lead at Old Trafford.

Wayne Rooney acrobatically levelled for United early in the second half, before Gylfi Sigurdsson fired home to give the visitors all three points.

“When you have preparation, win everything, then lose your first match, it cannot be worse,” Van Gaal said. “We have built up a lot of confidence. It will be smashed because of this.”

It was also the first time United had lost at Old Trafford on the opening day of the season since a 3-2 defeat against Ipswich Town in 1972.

Eight years after Van Gaal’s United debut, Ten Hag followed in the footsteps of his compatriot by losing 2-1 at home in his first game in charge.

United began the 2022/23 season by welcoming Brighton to Old Trafford and Ten Hag’s team news raised a few eyebrows, with Christian Eriksen debuting in the false nine role and Cristiano Ronaldo named on the bench.

They were outplayed by the Seagulls in the opening period and Pascal Gross’ first-half double saw them trailing 2-0 at the interval.

Ronaldo was brought on in the second half and Alexis Mac Allister’s own goal halved the deficit, but United were unable to find an equaliser.

Despite wanting to stay at Sporting CP until the end of the 2024/25 season, Amorim ultimately agreed to take over at United in November 2024.

His first game was against Ipswich Town at Portman Road and it got off to a perfect start, with Marcus Rashford scoring inside the opening two minutes.

But the hosts were the better side for the rest of the first half, and Omari Hutchinson scored the equaliser just before the break.

United dominated possession in the second half but didn’t create many chances, and they needed a brilliant save from Andre Onana to prevent Ipswich from taking all three points.

One of five former United players on this list, Fletcher was placed in caretaker charge following the decision to sack Amorim in January 2026.

His first game saw United face Burnley at Turf Moor, and he immediately moved away from the Portuguese coach’s 3-4-3 set-up in favour of a back four.

But the change in formation didn’t have an immediate impact, and they fell behind in the 13th minute when Ayden Heaven turned into his own net from a Bashir Humphreys cross.

Benjamin Sesko netted a brace in a 10-minute spell at the start of the second half, before the hosts drew level with a brilliant strike from Jaidon Anthony.

Shea Lacey hit the crossbar in the final stages as United dominated proceedings, but they were unable to find a winner.

Rangnick agreed a six-month deal to become United’s interim manager in November 2021, but work permit issues delayed his arrival.

The German, who is renowned for a high-pressing style, was finally in the dugout for Crystal Palace’s trip to Old Trafford at the start of the following month.

His influence was clear in a breathless opening 30 minutes as United pressed from the front and played at a noticeably quicker tempo.

Their performance petered off after that strong start, but a 77th-minute strike from Fred gave United a fully deserved 1-0 victory.

“With just the one training session, I was really impressed,” Rangnick said after the game. “We did much better than expected.”

The first competitive game in the post-Ferguson era saw Moyes lead United out at Wembley to face Wigan in the 2013 Community Shield.

United were strong favourites against a side that had just been relegated from the Premier League, and Robin van Persie headed home the opening goal inside the opening six minutes.

Van Persie’s deflected strike doubled United’s lead on the hour mark, and that signalled a comfortable end to proceedings.

The celebrations were mooted, and it proved to be both the first and last piece of silverware that Moyes lifted at United.

Van Nistelrooy joined Ten Hag’s coaching staff in the summer of 2024 and took over as interim manager a few weeks later.

He delivered goals throughout his playing career at Old Trafford, and his first game in the dugout was a seven-goal thriller against Leicester City in the Carabao Cup.

Casemiro and Bruno Fernandes both netted braces in the last-16 tie, while Alejandro Garnacho also got on the scoresheet in a 5-2 home win.

Despite still being part of United’s first-team squad, Giggs was named interim manager after Moyes was sacked in April 2014.

His first match in the dugout saw United face Norwich City at Old Trafford, and he was met with a rapturous reception as he emerged from the tunnel.

But United started slowly, and the first half looked set to finish goalless until Danny Welbeck was felled in the area and Wayne Rooney converted a 43rd-minute penalty.

Rooney doubled their lead at the start of a much improved second half before Juan Mata came off the bench to score a brace of his own, giving United a comfortable 4-0 victory.

One of two Carrick entries on this list, the former United midfielder was initially placed in temporary charge after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was sacked in November 2021.

He began his first spell as interim manager with an away game against Villarreal in the Champions League group stage, and David De Gea kept United in the game with two great saves either side of halftime.

Carrick’s substitutions helped change the flow of the game, and Cristiano Ronaldo broke the deadlock in the 78th minute before Jadon Sancho made it 2-0 in injury time.

The win against the Yellow Submarine saw United secure top spot in their Champions League group with a game to spare.

Despite winning the FA Cup final in 2016, Van Gaal was sacked by United and Mourinho was in charge when they returned to Wembley for the Community Shield.

Mourinho went into the game having lost his three previous Community Shields and United had to face the then-reigning Premier League champions Leicester City.

United started brightly in the traditional curtain-raiser, and Jesse Lingard added to his FA Cup final-winning goal with a stunning solo effort.

Jamie Vardy equalised at the start of the second half before Zlatan Ibrahimovic marked his competitive United debut by heading home the winner in the 83rd minute.

Mourinho’s third-season syndrome kicked in once again, and Solskjaer replaced him on an initial interim basis in December 2018.

His first game in the dugout saw him return to the Cardiff City Stadium, having had a 30-game spell in charge of the Welsh side in 2014.

Marcus Rashford fired United in front with a brilliant free-kick in the third minute, while goals from Ander Herrera and Anthony Martial gave the visitors a 3-1 lead at half-time.

A second-half brace from Jesse Lingard made it a comprehensive win as United scored five goals in a Premier League game for the first time since Ferguson retired.

Carrick and Solskjaer were both interviewed by United in January 2026, with the former ultimately being handed the job until the end of the season.

But he began his second spell in the Old Trafford dugout with a daunting first assignment: a Manchester derby.

The manager was still able to oversee an immediate improvement, and second-half goals from Bryan Mbeumo and Patrick Dorgu gave United a 2-0 win over Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City.

It was a thoroughly deserved victory for United, who also hit the woodwork twice and had three goals ruled out for offside.

“It’s an easy thing to say but I couldn’t ask for any more from the boys,” Carrick said after the game. “They gave everything.

“We only had three days to prepare and they took everything on board, tactically, and to be able to deal with it emotionally was exactly as we hoped for.”

#1482. Ranking all 27 signings Tottenham made under Mauricio Pochettino

Mauricio Pochettino may have operated with one hand tied behind his back at times when it comes to signing players for Tottenham – but how did the transfers he was able to complete fare?

Spurs famously failed to sign a single player in the summer of 2018 and followed that with a similarly fruitless January, but ironically it was when Pochettino did get money to spend in 2019 that things started to go wrong.

He’ll be hoping his new recruitment team at Manchester United can give him a good helping hand in his new job, but it might take a while before United overtake Spurs as the club people most easily associate Pochettino with.

Pochettino signed 27 players in his five years in charge of Tottenham, and we’ve ranked each of those signings, starting off with the stinkers.

Tottenham actually beat Arsenal to the €12million signing of N’Jie from Lyon, all for the sake of eight substitute appearances in the Premier League before he was sent back to Ligue 1.

Cameroon boss Hugo Broos offered an insight into why the winger’s move to north London possibly didn’t work out when accusing him of not working hard enough.

“He must change his attitude and put in the work required if he is to turn the qualities he possesses into success at the top level,” Broos said.

“Even Ronaldo or Messi are always working hard; him thinking that he’s the best doesn’t work, it doesn’t work in Marseille either.”

Clinton N'Jie's shot against Atlético Madrid in all its glory.

— Football on TNT Sports (@footballontnt) May 16, 2018

“I have not wasted my time in England.” As far as an evaluation of your time at a club goes, Stambouli’s doesn’t sound too promising.

Stambouli arrived at White Hart Lane with a burgeoning reputation after helping Montpellier win Ligue 1 and often captaining the side at the age of 23.

But the midfielder failed to make an impression at Spurs and was sold after just one season, somehow at a profit, to PSG, where he also lasted a solitary campaign.

We have an element of sympathy for Janssen. Being a backup striker for a team who don’t really play to your strengths seems like a hard gig. But it was made even harder in this instance by the fact Janssen was just a bit… erm… crap.

To be fair to him, he deserved plenty of credit for somehow wrangling the No.9 shirt for the second half of the 2018-19 season despite not appearing for the side since August 2017.

In 2019 he was sold to Monterrey in Mexico for a reported £6.3million, £10.7million less than Spurs had paid for him three years earlier.

This is a bit awkward because Fazio was generally quite good after leaving Tottenham – Gabriel Batistuta even named his fellow Argentine among some of the best defenders in the world in 2017.

But getting sent off twice within the first four months of his Spurs career set a tone which never really changed.

Burnt by the signing of a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1, Spurs decided to replace Clinton N’Jie with Nkoudou, a young, unproven winger from Ligue 1.

He cost them £11million and was sold three years later for £4.6million after a grand total of 10 Premier League appearances.

But we did like his self-effacing follow-up to assisting Harry Winks’ late winner against Fulham in a rare Premier League appearance.

— GK NKoudou ⚡️ (@gknkoudou) January 20, 2019

Given it was Daniel Levy who decided Spurs should sign Clarke from Leeds, there’s an argument to say he shouldn’t even be on this list.

Either way, he cost £10million, was not wanted by Pochettino – at least initially – and never played a single minute of league football for Spurs.

Loans at Leeds, QPR and Stoke did not work out, but he showed signs of improvement while out at Sunderland in 2021-22 and helped them back into the second tier. Still, £10million.

READ MORE: Man Utd reunion? An XI of Pochettino signings sealed by Paul Mitchell

Aurier was quite an expensive signing from PSG and failed to establish himself ahead of Kieran Trippier at right-back.

Then Trippier was sold and was very, very sorely missed.

Tottenham’s record signing at the time, Ndombele provided us with some wonderful moments of skill. But for £60million, we really expected more than a few moments.

Again, good moments. And a spell of genuinely influential form under Jose Mourinho in 2020.

But nowhere near enough to justify the £42million Spurs forked out in combined loan and transfer fees.

In 2015, Yedlin arrived at Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

In 2016, Yedlin left Tottenham as a very fast, young player who lacked the technical and tactical qualities to really shine at the highest level of the game.

He only ever made one appearance, but Spurs sold him at a profit to Newcastle, where he made over 100 appearances before going to Galatasaray. That profit alone has shifted him a few places up this ranking.

Lopez never actually played for Tottenham, but he did give our good friend Matt Stead at Football365 the opportunity to regularly upset people by writing that the goalkeeper was an Irishman called Paul O’Pez.

Plus, he was only ever signed on loan to be third-choice goalkeeper so, unlike some of the others, at least he didn’t do anything wrong.

Michel Vorm was fine and these kind of signings are boringly necessary. Sorry.

We also really enjoyed his explanation for signing a new deal at the club in the summer of 2018: “I didn’t have other options.”

He left in 2019 and failed to find another club that summer. But after an injury to Hugo Lloris a few months later, he returned to Spurs on a short-term deal to provide cover. He made one more appearance before retiring in 2020.

Another one who goes in the early promise, a few good games, then not much else category. The saving grace with Foyth is the £5million or so profit they made on him.

We were absolutely convinced Sanchez had all the attributes to succeed at Spurs – and potentially to become one of the best centre-backs in the league – when he signed from Ajax in 2017. And he played more than 200 games for Spurs in the end.

But we can’t help but feel slightly disappointed at how it all turned out for him. He didn’t quite reach his potential. A shame.

Pochettino really liked Gazzaniga, who hails from the same town in Argentina as the former Spurs boss and also played under him at Southampton.

“It was a bit crazy,” Gazzaniga told ESPN in 2018. “Mauricio had a relationship with my granddad and especially my dad, because they played against each other with Instituto and Newell’s Old Boys, and my uncle went to school with him when they were children. It was a big coincidence.”

Coincidence is perhaps not the word we’d choose.

Anyway, Gazzaniga was more than serviceable when he turned out for Spurs, even if he never established himself as a genuine contender to Hugo Lloris.

Signed for £4.3million from Cologne in 2015, Wimmer was a reliable backup in his two seasons at Spurs and impressed when thrust into the team following an injury to Jan Vertonghen early in 2016.

He helped Spurs win six and draw two of a nine-game run in the team, earning himself a new five-year deal in the process, but he was back to being a back-up once Vertonghen returned and only made five Premier League appearances in 2016-17.

Somehow, however, Spurs sold him to Stoke for £18million. Halfway through the season he was on an individual fitness regime and not being considered for the first team even as Stoke hurtled towards relegation.

Starting a petition to re-sign Kevin Wimmer for the sole purpose of keeping Son happy, if anyone is interested. https://t.co/z9L7lKCyiB

— James Harris (@JamesCHarris97) February 3, 2019

It took a while but, at the back end of the 2021-22 season, Ryan Sessegnon finally started to show that he could be a good long-term option for Spurs.

Did he actually become the long-term option for Spurs? No. He didn’t justify his £25million fee, but has at least established himself elsewhere in the Premier League back at Fulham.

Watching Llorente for Spurs was at times pretty uncomfortable.

We’ve already said with regards to Janssen that playing as a backup striker and being expected to score goals when thrown into a team which hardly plays to your strengths, with little match practice, must be pretty difficult.

Llorente definitely made it look pretty difficult. But he also scored a few goals – as he did throughout his career for Europe’s biggest teams – and his hold-up play was excellent.

And his contributions to Spurs’ run to the Champions League in 2019 mean that, despite being released at the end of that season, he’ll always be remembered fondly.

Injuries hampered Wanyama, but the former Southampton man was excellent in his debut season at Spurs after joining for only £11million, helping the north Londoners finish second in the Premier League.

Quite frankly, we would have paid £11million for this goal alone.

One year ago today, Victor Wanyama delivered the ball back into the Liverpool net with real interest. https://t.co/nku4aiyZW6

— Football Ramble (@FootballRamble) February 4, 2019

For a long while it looked like Sissoko would be at the other end of this list, hovering somewhere around Stambouli and Fazio.

After all, for a club which hardly splashes the cash, a £30million outlay on a player who started just eight Premier League games in his debut campaign tends to suggest a bit of a f*ck up.

But, slowly but surely, Pochettino began to iron out the inconsistency and unpredictability and turn Sissoko from a punchline of a right-winger into a combative, all legs-and-lungs central midfielder.

There was plenty of excitement when Spurs parted with £25million to land the forward from PSG, but it took the Brazil international six months to adapt to English football.

After initially underwhelming, Moura shone in his first full season, most notably scoring that incredible second-half hat-trick at Ajax to fire Spurs to the Champions League final.

He was ultimately usurped by Dejan Kulusevski, but we were still tempted to make him No.1 for this reaction alone.

An emotional Lucas Moura hears the commentary from Brazil of his winner for Spurs at Ajax (via @Esp_Interativo) pic.twitter.com/xr2a4sLZez

— Guardian sport (@guardian_sport) May 9, 2019

The absolute definition of a solid club servant. And Spurs only paid £13.5million for him and Vorm combined. Bargain.

Trippier wasn’t able to maintain his 2017-18 form following the World Cup, but perhaps the right-back used up a career’s worth of highs in Russia.

And the fact Spurs were able to sell him to Atletico Madrid for £20million in 2019 tells you he was still pretty decent in 2018-19. Considering he only cost £3.5million, it’s safe to say he goes down as a success.

Another player who seems to attract both over-the-top praise and criticism, Dier was popular with Pochettino and forced himself into the team under all of the managers who’ve followed the Argentine. That’s not a coincidence.

A largely unknown £4million signing from Sporting Lisbon going on to appear over 300 times for Spurs and becoming an established England international generally signifies a very good bit of business.

He stagnated big time during his last couple of years at Spurs, but just think back to those heady days in 2016 when he was playing off Harry Kane, making late runs into the box and finding the net with unerring regularity. Wonderful stuff.

✨🌏✨ A world-class goal from Dele Alli ✨🌏✨#GoalOfTheDay pic.twitter.com/eJHJk5t4sD

— Premier League (@premierleague) September 17, 2021

It’s easy to forget quite how complicated a transfer saga Alderweireld’s signing became for Tottenham, with the defender joining from Atletico Madrid despite Southampton wanting to exercise their option to sign the player on a permanent deal after a successful loan spell.

The £11.4million deal was worth all the headaches, however, as he quickly struck up one of the best defensive partnerships in the league with fellow Belgian and former Ajax team-mate Jan Vertonghen.

Quite possibly the most fun and undoubtedly one of the most brilliant footballers in the Premier League in his prime.

Thank God they didn’t sell him after a difficult first season. We absolutely love him.

#1481. Scotland’s Pocognoli era starts with encouraging signs but familiar issues in front of goal

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant said: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

“They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a big game again on Tuesday so it’s important to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

“We’ve had a great week. A new manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

“I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”

Pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

Scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

Lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

Oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

How has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

Another change is here for Scotland, with Gannon-Doak on to replace Hickey.

Another big chance for Scotland. This time Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie goes close.Slovenia 0-0 Scotland - watch the closing stages on BBC One. pic.twitter.com/xMe5gRNgEr

From the resulting corner, Oblak is there again to thwart McBurnie’s point-blank header. The referee then blows his whistle to relieve the pressure on Slovenia. Somehow, the scoreline remains goalless.

The hosts make another double change as Sporar and Brekalo depart for Vipotnik and Balkovec.

Welsh spots Bowie’s run and threads a perfectly-weighted pass through to the forward. From an unfavourable angle, the substitute’s one-on-one attempt is blocked by Oblak.

Another massive chance for Scotland! McGinn’s searching corner is met by Hickey, who flicks a header wide of the far post. Scotland’s second-half performance deserves a goal.

Pocognoli orders Scotland’s first alteration of the game, with Bowie replacing Ure up top.

Hickey finds himself very high up the pitch and tries to tee up Ure with a cushioned header, but there isn’t enough power on the pass.

Gilmour and Ure link up effectively on the counter, but the latter’s pull-back is intercepted by Drkusic.

Slovenia then make two changes as Zabukovnik and Zec replace Elsnik and Drkusic.

McGinn strides forward and tries to find Ure, but Slovenia rush back to scramble it clear. Scotland are really pushing for the opening goal.

Gilmour and McBurnie play a devastating one-two, allowing the midfielder to advance into the penalty area. He shoots and aims for the far corner, but his placed effort is collected impressively by Oblak, who makes another crucial intervention.

The second half has started as the first ended, with Scotland applying all of the pressure. Slovenia have Oblak to thank for the goalless scoreline.

McBurnie and Oblak both challenge for the ball, with the Scotsman bumping into the goalkeeper, giving Slovenia a goal kick. The decision is met by a chorus of boos from the away fans.

McBurnie latches onto a loose ball and skips away from Drkusic’s sliding challenge. One-on-one, the striker tries to round Oblak, but the Slovenian goalkeeper does sensationally to apprehend him. Upon reflection, it looks like McBurnie should have just shot and tried to put the ball between Oblak’s legs. He did the hard part, but lacked a clinical finish.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb

McGinn brilliantly turns Drkusic on the halfway line and then tees up Gilmour. The Napoli midfielder tries to float a pass over to the onrushing Robertson, but he hits the switch of play straight out for a throw-in. In defence of Gilmour, the pitch really doesn’t look in the best condition, with various players struggling regarding their weight of pass.

We are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Pocognoli’s Scotland finished the half as the better side, but an opening goal has proved to be elusive. At times, they’ve looked suspect defensively and have lacked rhythm going forward. However, Pocognoli’s squad have only been together for a few days and are playing in a new system. Can they produce a more inspired second-half performance?

Despite Scotland’s late push for an opening goal at the end of the first half, the two sides head in level at the break. Slovenia started on the front-foot, with Sporar and Drkusic both going close for the hosts, before Ure struck the post to be denied a dream debut goal.

HALF TIME: Slovenia 0-0 Scotland.No goals at the break in Ljubljana.#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/6VGFRprBiz

Ure strikes the woodwork! The Sevilla striker is agonisingly close to a debut goal for his country. He cuts inside to work some space and fires a low effort at goal, but his shot hits the post.

Scotland's best chance of the game so far 😯 Sevilla striker and debutant Robbie Ure strikes the post just before half-time.However, it remains goalless at the break.📺 Watch Slovenia v Scotland on BBC One 🇸🇮 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 pic.twitter.com/fm1wH2fOej

Much better from Scotland! McGinn turns his marker and clips a wonderful pass over to Ure, who has drifted out wide. The ball is then delivered into the box toward McGinn, whose header bounces off McBurnie. Hickey is arriving to pounce on the loose ball, but the wing-back’s effort is blocked by the Slovenian defence.

Robertson picks up the game’s first yellow card for an off-the-ball incident. The Scotland captain is clearly very unhappy with the decision as we await to see a replay. Nevertheless, the action resumes with a Slovenia free-kick.

Slovenia go close again as a corner is whipped in. Drkusic wins the header at the near post and it bounces off the outside of the near post. That is definitely another warning sign for Scotland.

Matko goes on the outside of Welsh, and from a tight angle, he shoots, but his fizzed effort saves the side netting of the near post. Some fans behind the goal cheer because they think it’s gone in, but their view has really deceived them.

It’s been a quiet afternoon for both goalkeepers so far, with neither yet to make a noteworthy save. On a couple of occasions, Slovenia have had encouraging opportunities to get the ball into the Scotland’s box, but the deliveries have been overhit and poorly executed.

Similarly to Scotland, Slovenia are also playing a tremendously high-line. Unlike Slovenia, Scotland have been unable to find the right pass in behind the home side’s defence. Gilmour then carelessly gives the ball away as Scotland’s latest spell of possession ends.

Since Slovenia wasted that 14th-minute chance, Scotland have grown into the contest and are beginning to look comfortable in possession. However, they’re still waiting to craft their first notable opening here.

The hosts miss a huge chance! Once again, Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s incredibly high line and then fires a low cross into the penalty area. Sporar then beats McKenna to the delivery, but taps his close-range effort wide of the far post from inside the six-yard box. That’s a massive let-off for Scotland...

Matko is unleashed by a drilled pass then pierces through a gap between Robertson and Welsh. The Slovenia winger drives into the penalty area and tries to find either Sturm or Sporar with a cross, but Hendry does magnificently to make a last-ditch clearance.

Slovenia have the ball in the net, but the offside flag is up. Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s defence and slides a low cross into Sporar’s path. The striker then sweeps a composed first-time effort into the top corner. It’s a brilliant finish, but Sturm was miles offside in the build-up.

Gunn comes out confidently to collect a looping cross, before the ball is launched forward in McBurnie’s direction. The Hull City striker and Ure are playing really close to each other, very much like an old-school front-two.

Slovenia forward Sturm is wiped out by Hendry’s wild early challenge. The Scotland defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a booking. Welsh then heads the resulting set-piece away and out for a corner.

The hosts get us underway in the Slovenian capital. Can Pocognoli begin his Scotland tenure with a Nations League victory?

Both teams are out on the pitch in Ljubljana. We are moments away from the start of the Pocognoli era.

New Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli sings Flower of Scotland as he takes charge of the national side for the first time 🎶 🇸🇮 Slovenia v Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 is live on BBC One now.#BBCFootball #NationsLeague pic.twitter.com/I2aeqYkNGB

With just over 10 minutes until kick-off, here’s a reminder of both teams’ line-ups.

Slovenia: Oblak, Brekalo, Bijol, Drkusic, Janza, Karnicnik, Cerin, Elsnik, Matko, Sturm, Sporar.

Subs: Kelly, Bain, Binks, Doig, Christie, Miller, McPake, Doak, Graham, Bowie, Patterson, Montgomery.

"Let's go!" 👏#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/HBvPJdFkFb

Luis Binks of Brondby, as well as Colby Donovan and Josh McPake, who play for Celtic and Hearts respectively, are all amongst the substitutes. This hopeful trio are all in line for their Scotland debuts if they enter the action later this afternoon.

Slovenski navijači se že zbirajo 👊🇸🇮#SrceBije 🇸🇮 pic.twitter.com/dM9UArGgl3

How much do the Tartan Army really know about new Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli? 🤔 We sent Jonathan Sutherland around Ljubljana to find out.📺 Watch 🇸🇮 Slovenia v Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 on Saturday on BBC One from 13:45 BST. pic.twitter.com/KSurjSmKwL

'We're not going to be perfect right away but we still demand results'Scotland's Lewis Ferguson as the team begins a new era under Sebastien Pocognoli 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/42WCJh66gc

Slovenia: Oblak, Brekalo, Bijol, Drkusic, Janza, Karnicnik, Cerin, Elsnik, Matko, Sturm, Sporar.

Subs: Vidovsek, Leban, Balkovec, Zabukovnik, Kuzmic, Begic, Lovric, Celar, Svetlin, Zec, Vipotnik, Horvat.

On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A new-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Sebastien Pocognoli's first Scotland XI to take on Slovenia 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿Watch the game live on BBC One Scotland from 13:45 BST 📺#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/OnfWR7Gp8C

The squad's here 🏟️#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/IUiWhTHUT4

🚨 Znana je začetna enajsterica Slovenije za tekmo s Škotsko! 👊🇸🇮#SrceBije 🇸🇮 | #NationsLeague 🇪🇺 pic.twitter.com/rjEdMyyYGO

Debutants Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh are each poised for their first international cap. Billy Gilmour returns to the starting XI after missing the World Cup through injury and Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance for Scotland since 2021.

Sébastien Pocognoli's first Scotland starting XI 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/JC6RGOq1QJ

“The first game is always a special game so you have to bring the mental aspect in for the players and for the staff.

“A good result can help but the most important thing is we see things that we work on through the week. I hope is we apply that well then we will get the result which will be the perfect mix.

“I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of new players.

“We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his new role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1480. The 9 players with a €1billion release clause: Yamal, Mbappe, Vinicius…

Barcelona and Real Madrid get around Spain’s mandatory release by protecting their top stars with a €1billion release clause that would be beyond even Saudi Pro League clubs.

Some of the best players in the world – and others very much not so – have gigantic clauses in their contracts.

Here are the nine players who reportedly have a €1billion release clause in their contracts.

The midfielder set Barcelona’s precedent with a record €1billion when he signed his a contract extension in October 2021.

After putting his injury woes behind him, Pedri got back to his best as a key cog in 2024-25’s treble chase under Hansi Flick.

Arguably the best midfielder in world football right now, in January 2025 Barcelona tied down his future to 2030. His release clause hasn’t been touched.

Barcelona’s homegrown starlet followed Pedri’s lead and signed a deal running to 2030 – with a new €1billion release clause.

Unlike Pedri, he isn’t a regular starter this season but he’s evidently seen as a big part of the club’s future.

Barcelona signed their prized asset to the maximum three years for a 16-year-old in 2023. Even back then they recognised his potential and made sure he wouldn’t be going anywhere with a €1billion release clause.

He’s now under contract until 2031 and firmly established as one of the best players in the world.

TRY A QUIZ: Can you name the last 20 players to break the world transfer record?

Kounde attracts links with Premier League clubs fairly often, but Barcelona are in a strong negotiating position. He remains contracted in Catalonia until 2030 and included the increasingly commonplace €1billion release clause when they signed him from Sevilla in 2022.

The Brazilian signed a new contract at the Bernabeu in 2022 with a €1billion clause, which remains in place after his latest renewal earlier this year.

There have been times when people have wondered if he’d move on, and if it might actually be beneficial for all concerned, but he remains rooted in Madrid for the foreseeable.

A rare €100million investment that looks worth it, Madrid included the largely symbolic release clause in the England international’s contract when he was signed from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2023.

He’s under contract with Real Madrid until 2029 and it’s difficult to envisage him going anywhere else anytime soon.

QUIZ: Can you name the 25 most expensive transfers of all time?

A proper Galactico, Mbappe was always going to have the classic sky-high release clause factored into his deal following his long-awaited arrival from Paris Saint-Germain.

At least that’s according to Spanish outlet COPE. We have no reason to doubt it.

Signed as a free agent, the World Cup winner signed a five-year deal running to 2029. You can only imagine Florentino Perez’s face if a club was audacious enough to try and prise him away now. Never gonna happen.

Madrid believed they were signing one of the top prospects in European football when they signed Camavinga as a teenager from Rennes back in 2021.

His versatility has certainly proven useful, while his early promise earned him a bumper payrise in a bumper new contract in 2023 with a new release clause that rose to €1billion.

There are some question marks over how he’s developed and whether he’ll truly be the future of the Madrid midfield, but he’s established himself pretty well.

Rodrygo signed his last contract extension back in 2023, a five-year deal running through to 2028.

There have been times of speculation over him leaving, but he remains committed to Los Blancos and can’t exactly go anywhere while coming back from a serious injury.

#1479. Pressing with intensity, getting runners beyond Kane and playing like a 'Premier League team': How Thomas Tuchel's new-look England dismantled Spain - and what he's learned from cowardly retreat against Argentina

Published: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026

By the end of the World Cup, it felt as if Argentina had ripped the mask off Thomas Tuchel’s England only to reveal Gareth Southgate’s England standing there blinking right back at them.

On the biggest stage, against the biggest teams, under the biggest pressure, England wilted as they always did. They sat back, they were too cautious, and they lost. And yet, ever since, Tuchel has turned England into a free-scoring winning machine, topped off by a famous victory in Madrid, ending Spain’s 43-match unbeaten streak.

In the six games since the summer, England have scored 19 goals and conceded six. Five of those have been against the world champions.

Yes, this was the Nations League and not a World Cup semi-final. No, it wasn’t at the end of a gruelling five weeks of heat, humidity and altitude. And, yes, it was only a terrific late double save from James Trafford that stopped this being yet another tale of self-sabotaging England, thanks to Elliot Anderson’s red card, blowing another lead when under pressure.

But, this time, England did see it out. They secured Tuchel’s biggest win as England boss and, in doing so, showed us just how he’s been able to get his side playing his way.

Harry Kane leads the England celebrations after his side's victory over Spain in Madrid on Sunday night

Remember when everyone used to lose their minds whenever Harry Kane dropped deep in big games under Southgate? He’s our bloody striker, for goodness sake. Get in the box!

After England’s defeat by Spain in the Euro 2024 final two years ago, Opta posted on X that Kane had touched the ball just once in the opposition box across both that game and their previous final heartbreak against Italy three years earlier.

‘One fewer than Jack Grealish,’ the post continued. ‘Grealish played 21 minutes in the 2020 final and didn't make the Euro 2024 squad.’

Ballon d’Or winner Kane has made it quite clear since that he doesn’t need to spend all his time in the box to influence games. When he drops deeper, Kane is able to show the full extent of his creativity and range of passing.

The main problem with the ploy under Southgate, however, was that Kane rarely had the team-mates to make the right runs ahead of him. He was surrounded by players who wanted to take up similar positions. Just look at the average position maps (below) from England’s loss to Spain at Euro 2024 compared to last night.

The average position map of England’s players in the loss to Spain at Euro 2024 show how Kane dropped deep, without team-mates making runs for him to exploit

...whereas on Sunday night he had runners - Anthony Gordon, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers - around and beyond him

Two years ago, the only player who averaged their touches ahead of Kane was Bukayo Saka. Jude Bellingham was out wide. Kobbie Mainoo and Phil Foden were basically in Kane’s shadow.

On Sunday night, he had Anthony Gordon, the brilliant, belligerent Bellingham and Morgan Rogers all ahead of him – and nearly even Ben White.

That desire, and instruction, to flock forward under Tuchel has made such a difference.

Take England’s third goal (below). Kane has the ball outside the area. Rogers is bombing on to his left. Gordon, who started as a winger but finds himself occupying the central spaces Kane leaves behind, darts into the box and points to where he wants it.

Bellingham is demanding the ball, too, showing Kane he wants it to feet. Even Anderson is charging into the box. Kane finds Bellingham, who feeds the unseen White, sprinting forward on the overlap to finish.

Kane picks up the ball and is met with an array of options in front of him, ahead of England's third goal

He did similar in the win against Croatia a few days earlier, too.

Kane collects the ball deep with four bodies ahead of him, including full backs Lewis Hall and Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It his raking pass to the back post which allows Bellingham to set up Rogers to finish.

Kane's lofted pass to Rogers (top right) leads to a goal against Croatia for Bellingham (edge of box)

England’s fluidity in the final third is bamboozling defences. That is how you get the best of Kane’s creativity.

Football is changing, so Pep Guardiola told us all in January last year. The modern game is now how teams like Bournemouth and Brighton play. The current Premier League table would suggest he had a point.

Over the past few years in the English top flight, we have seen teams move away from an obsession with keeping the ball for the sake of it and turn towards a far faster, more aggressive and more physical style of play.

Tuchel wants to take from that playbook. ‘We're at our best when we're free, physically overpowering and making it Premier League-level,’ said Kane after last month's 7-0 rout of Croatia.

In the six matches since the World Cup, Tuchel’s England are having much less of the ball than they did at the start of his reign – and now less even than under Southgate.

The key is they are becoming ever more direct with it. Tuchel wants his England to play out of the back with short passes, entice opponents on to them, but then move it through the lines at speed.

Since the World Cup, England are playing far fewer passes, but more of them into the box – to find those runners. A higher percentage of them forward. More direct attacks, moving the ball up the field at a quicker speed.

On Sunday night, they showed how Tuchel wants his side to press. ‘We were hungry in the opposition half,’ said the England boss at full time.

A fine example of that (below) came just after just six minutes. Declan Rice gives his Arsenal team-mate Martín Zubimendi no time at all on the ball inside his own area, charging him down, and forcing him to play out to another Gunner in Mikel Merino. But he, too, is being harassed by Anderson and eventually England win it back and set up Kane for a chance that he fizzes wide.

A half-fit Rice was unable to apply that pressure in the summer.

Declan Rice charges forward to close down Martin Zubimendi who has possession just inside the Spanish box with Kane and Bellingham already engaged in a high press...

...Zubimendi passes to Mikel Merino but Elliot Anderson is all over him and it leads to Kane shot that just fizzes wide

So much of this improvement under Tuchel into a side capable of blowing teams away can be put down to another abstract word he used post-match in Madrid: ‘brave’.

Tuchel talked in the last international break of ‘unlocking the next level’, and taking ‘calculated risks’ with a ‘man-to-man’ press in the opposition half.

Under Southgate, and certainly in the cowardly retreat against Argentina in the summer, England showed little bravery either with the ball or without it and frequently showed too much respect to those big nations.

Too safe with the ball, too afraid to give it away, and too fearful to try to win it back in case you leave yourself open.

That appears to be changing, too. There was a moment at the start of the second half when Bellingham tried a risky through-ball to Rogers, which failed to find its man, instead of another simple ball out wide.

It handed Spain possession cheaply. But England didn’t care because they just pounced again. Spain couldn’t deal with it. In the first half, Spain completed just 84 per cent of their passes in their own half – a place where they are usually able to knock it about at will – their lowest completion rate according to Opta since the 2010 World Cup. They didn’t have a shot on target until the penalty.

England’s defence has long been seen as the weak spot and, under Southgate, it felt as though he always would rather his attacking talents not be too frivolous for fear of exposing it.

Thomas Tuchel and Kane direct England's players to keep on the front foot during the win over Spain

Tuchel is doing the opposite. England’s expected goals soared from 1.7 per game under Southgate from the 2022 World Cup to the end of his reign, to 2.2 under Tuchel’s until this summer’s tournament. Since then, it’s jumped again to 2.8 but at the cost of what they are conceding. In his early days, England coughed up fewer good chances than under Southgate but since the World Cup has more than doubled.

He will want to get that down, of course, but when you are creating so much – and have an array of top finishers to see them off – how much will that matter to Tuchel?

Even he’s getting braver. His decision to take off Gordon for Konsa and chuck as many defenders on during England’s shrinking against Argentina looked a decision that would forever haunt Tuchel’s tenure.

Against Spain, Kane made way but Tuchel ended the game with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin on the pitch. Against Spain, he held his nerve.
